function.name: requests_get
function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary mapping protocol names to URLs of the proxies.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

message.content:
The “triangulation metrics” function is designed to evaluate how well a set of points (e.g., sensor locations, survey markers, or other spatial references) covers a target area or volume. In practice, it calculates several key statistics that describe the quality of the triangulation:

| Metric | What it measures | Typical interpretation |
|--------|------------------|--------------------------|
| **Average edge length** | Mean distance between connected points in the triangulation mesh | Shorter edges → finer resolution; longer edges → coarser coverage |
| **Maximum edge length** | Longest distance between any two connected points | Helps identify gaps or poorly sampled regions |
| **Minimum edge length** | Shortest distance between any two connected points | Detects overly dense clusters that may be redundant |
| **Aspect ratio** | Ratio of longest to shortest side of each triangle | Values close to 1 indicate well‑shaped triangles; high values signal skinny, poorly conditioned triangles |
| **Coverage density** | Number of points per unit area/volume | Higher density → more detailed representation |
| **Edge length variance** | Variability of edge lengths across the mesh | Low variance → uniform sampling; high variance → uneven distribution |
| **Number of triangles** | Total count of triangles in the mesh | Gives a sense of overall mesh complexity |
| **Mean triangle area** | Average area of triangles | Smaller areas → finer detail |
| **Maximum triangle area** | Largest triangle area | Identifies potential holes or under‑sampled zones |

These metrics help you decide whether your point set is dense enough, evenly distributed, and suitable for accurate interpolation or modeling. For example, if the maximum edge length is too large, you might need to add more points in that region. If the aspect ratio is high, you may need to adjust point placement to avoid poorly shaped triangles that can degrade numerical stability.

In short, the triangulation metrics function gives you a quick, quantitative snapshot of the spatial quality of your point set, enabling you to make informed decisions about data collection, refinement, or validation.
